newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S., China talks open on harmonious note.
newsitem.headline: U.S., China talks open on harmonious note.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and her Chinese counterpart opened their first talks on a harmonious note on Monday, praising the late Deng Xiaoping's role in forging Sino-American ties and expressing confidence they could work together despite disputes.

At a news conference before talks began with Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, Albright reiterated plans to raise China's troubling human rights record and push for improvements, including the release of political dissidents.
There have been such releases in the past "and obviously we would like to see more", Albright said.
But she signalled no imminent breakthrough, saying "we understand that this is a long process".
She also said human rights, a regular thorn in bilateral ties, would be one among many issues on the agenda.
Albright's first visit to Beijing since taking office went forward despite the death last Wednesday of Deng, China's paramount leader.

U.S. officials took this as a sign of China's intention to make progress in what until recently had been a deteriorating relationship. The recent past has been marked by bitter rows over Taiwan, trade, human rights and Chinese sales of arms and technology to countries like Pakistan and Iran.
"We will discuss areas where we are seeking further cooperation. We will discuss areas where we have differences and seek to narrow them," Albright said.
She and Qian also reasserted support for the Shanghai communique, signed nearly 25 years ago, which set the framework for the eventual forging of diplomatic ties.
Albright also offered condolences from U.S. President Bill Clinton and the American people to Deng's family and the Chinese people.

Deng "was a historic figure whose leadership produced the dramatic economic transformation that China has undergone these last two decades and who contributed much to the development of China-U.S. relations," Albright said.
Qian also paid tribute to Deng.
"It was under his personal guidance that we established diplomatic relations with the United States," he said.

"We are ready to work with the U.S. side to seize the current favourable opportunities, increase the dialogue, extend cooperation and enhance common understandings...so as to promote the healthy, steady and sustained devlopment of Sino-U.S. relations," Qian added.
The two officials will discuss a visit to Beijing soon by U.S. Vice President Al Gore and exchange visits by the U.S. and Chinese leaders.
Albright, on the last stop of a nine-nation tour, stepped off her plane only hours after Deng's body arrived at Beijing's Babaoshan cemetery for cremation.

"I'm going to talk across the board on all the issues that we have been talking about," she told staff at the U.S. embassy in Beijing shortly after her arrival. This would range from human rights to cooperation over North Korea and Cambodia as well as the environment, she said.
"My main mission is to engage with China and make them realise we want them to be part of our international community," she said.
U.S. officials tried to play down hopes of a breakthrough on thorny human rights issues, despite a New York Times report that the two sides appeared within striking range of a deal.
"I don't believe the story in the New York Times is accurate," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.
"We've received no indication that a major breakthough of the kind described in the New York Times is imminent."

The newspaper said under the possible deal China would agree to sign two key international covenants on human rights, release a represesentative group of at least eight prisoners and restart talks with the International Committee of the Red Cross for a programme of prison visits to determine the status of prisoners of conscience in China.
In return, Beijing could expect an end to the annual confrontation over its human rights record at the United Nations Commission on Human Rights in Geneva.
This package has been under discussion between Beijing and Washington for months, U.S. officials have said.
U.S. officials have said Washington does not expect Deng's death to bring any quick improvement in China's human rights and plans to proceed with a U.N. resolution faulting Beijing's record.

China is the last stop on Albright's nine-nation tour of European and Asian capitals, her first overseas trip since taking office last month. She will also meet President Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Peng. She is due to leave early on Tuesday, before Deng's memorial rites at Beijing's Great Hall of the People.
